one_liner: Abandoned C MVCC key-value engine (append-only, RAM-disk hybrid); self-reported 2.6x LevelDB random reads in 2013, never reproduced.
what_it_does: Embeddable transactional key-value/row storage library shipped as one amalgamated sophia.c plus sophia.h. It offers multiple databases sharing one write-ahead log, single- and multi-statement transactions under serializable snapshot isolation, upsert, cursors with prefix search, key expiry, hot backup and lz4/zstd compression. The API is a small generic object interface (sp_env, sp_document, sp_setstring/sp_setint, sp_set, sp_get, sp_cursor, sp_begin, sp_commit, sp_destroy) configured through string paths such as "db.test.compaction.cache", so it is not a drop-in for the LevelDB API.
how_it_is_fast: In the v1.2/2.x design each Node is one file of Branches; a Branch is a set of sorted, non-overlapping Regions with an in-memory region index, and each Node also keeps two in-memory key indexes that act like an LSM memtable. Writes are a WAL append plus an in-memory insert; a Branch operation later writes the sorted regions sequentially to the end of the node file, and a multi-threaded scheduler compacts a node's branches. A point read touches only one node and only the regions whose min/max range covers the key (amortized O(max_branch_count_per_node) disk reads), and pread or mmap access lets recently written branches be served from the page cache.
when_to_use: Studying or porting a storage-engine design: the README and architecture docs explain the region/branch/node layout, and the author's later engines (Amelia, Monotone) build on it.
Maintaining an existing application already on Sophia 2.2 whose storage format and workload are known to work.
Single-process programs that want cross-database SSI transactions and upsert from one dependency-free C file, and that can size db.compaction.cache from the memory-requirements tables.
Read-mostly workloads with small keys and values on SSD, the email-index case the author said the original homepage benchmark modelled.
when_not_to_use: Any new production system: the README says the project is no longer developed, the last code commit is 2019-01-25 (later commits edit the README), there are no tagged releases (issue #160 'Tag a New Release' is open) and 53 issues are open.

Write-heavy multi-threaded workloads: in issue #137 (2016) the maintainer said Sophia does not benefit from multithreaded access, and in an independent 2015 run HyperLevelDB 1.14 filled random keys about 1.5x faster than Sophia 1.1.

Large datasets with tight RAM: the documented cache requirement grows with write rate and capacity (for example 20,686 MB of cache for 1 MB/s of writes into 1000 GB on a 100 MB/s disk), and reopening a big database replays all logs (issue #137 reports a re-run stuck for over an hour).

Workloads that need proven crash safety: open issues include #171 (segfault with more than 6 key/value components), #54 (crash with multiple threads), #53 (crash in cursor iterator), #50 (deadlock when opening two cursors), #142 (broken backups) and #47/#48 (memory leaks).
Windows (open issue #96 asks for a Windows makefile; the makefile only handles Linux and Darwin).

integration.form: source-drop (amalgamated sophia.c and sophia.h generated by make) or static/shared lib
integration.dependencies: none per README and build docs; lz4 and zstd compression are built in, and open issues #153 and #179 say the bundled third-party code is old
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler with pthreads (documented build line: cc -O2 -DNDEBUG -std=c99 -pedantic -Wall -Wextra -pthread -c sophia.c)
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS per the makefile; other POSIX not documented; Windows unsupported; armv6l asked about in open issue #172
integration.thread_safety: Docs state all methods are thread-safe and atomic, with optimistic N-writer/M-reader concurrency, but the maintainer said in 2016 that it gains nothing from multiple threads, and a multi-thread crash report (#54) is still open.

gotchas: The default makefile always compiles with -DSS_INJECTION_ENABLE -g at -O2 and without -DNDEBUG, so fault-injection hooks ship in libsophia; build sophia.c yourself with the documented -O2 -DNDEBUG line for production.

The README headline 'O(1) worst case for read, write and range scan' describes the v1.1 design; the v1.2 docs give get as amortized O(max_branch_count_per_node) and full range traversal as O(total_region_count).

Multi-statement transactions can end in a 'lock' status (2) or a rollback (1); deadlocks are not resolved automatically (check the transaction's 'deadlock' field and destroy one side), and errors inside a transaction do not roll it back.

In the independent 2015 db_bench run, Sophia 1.1's fillrandsync row was 8.519 us/op against LevelDB 1.17's 6,370.717 us/op on the same SSD, far below a device flush latency, so Sophia's sync row probably did not fsync each write (log.sync is an option in 2.x); its random-fill database took about 26.2 GB on disk for 16 GB of data versus about 14.3 GB for LevelDB, and Sophia crashed before the read tests in both runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the catalogued LevelDB, HyperLevelDB and LMDB entries, pick Sophia only when you need multi-database SSI transactions and upsert in one small C file and can maintain it yourself; LMDB is maintained and read-optimized, and HyperLevelDB beat Sophia 1.1 on random fills in the only independent run found.
verified_claims_summary: The read claim rests on 2013 sphia.org figures relayed in a bitcoin-development mailing-list post (438,084 vs 167,476 random reads/sec against LevelDB on an unnamed SSD machine, 2.6x derived, seen as search snippets only, not reproduced by the poster, with a smaller gap to HyperLevelDB); no code, flags, CPU or versions are known. The only independent numbers found are Howard Chu's 2015 db_bench gist (hyc/87929fa3f95404512b4d: Samsung 830 SSD, 8 GB RAM, 160M records with 16-byte keys and 100-byte values, CPU and compiler not stated), where Sophia 1.1 fillrandom ran at 74,143 ops/sec versus LevelDB 1.17 at 48,930 (1.5x, derived) and HyperLevelDB 1.14 at 113,355, but Sophia crashed before any random-read test; with 4,000-byte values it filled at 7,368 versus 3,187 (2.3x, derived) and 24,836 for HyperLevelDB, and crashed again.
status_note: Abandoned: the author says it is no longer developed, the last code commit is 2019-01-25 and no release was ever tagged; it is BSD-2-Clause and one amalgamated C file, so it is easy to vendor for study or legacy use but not a sound choice for new production storage.
